content: Acyclovir has been shown to have the potential to shorten the duration of chickenpox illness, which may lead to reduced healthcare costs and decreased morbidity associated with the disease. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the evidence regarding the efficacy of acyclovir in alleviating chickenpox symptoms and shortening the illness duration, as well as to assess any complications of chickenpox and adverse effects related to acyclovir treatment as reported in clinical trials. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to September 2008. They also reviewed the reference lists of relevant articles. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials involving otherwise healthy children aged 0 to 18 years diagnosed with chickenpox. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the studies and evaluated their methodological quality using the Jadad scale and allocation concealment. Any disagreements were resolved through consensus. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and verified by another. Continuous data were analyzed using weighted mean differences (WMD), and results were pooled using a random-effects model. Due to the limited number of studies, statistical heterogeneity and publication bias were not formally assessed. Three studies met the inclusion criteria. The quality of the studies was rated as three (n=2) and four (n=1) on the Jadad scale. Acyclovir treatment was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the number of days with fever, with a mean reduction of 1.1 days (95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.3 to -0.9 days). Additionally, acyclovir reduced the maximum number of lesions by an average of 76 lesions (95% CI: -145 to -8 lesions). However, the results were less robust regarding the time to no new lesions and the time to relief of itching. There were no clinically significant differences between acyclovir and placebo in terms of complications related to chickenpox or adverse effects associated with the treatment. In conclusion, acyclovir appears to be effective in reducing the duration of fever and the maximum number of lesions in otherwise healthy children with chickenpox. However, its impact on the time to no new lesions and relief of itching was less convincing. The overall clinical significance of acyclovir treatment in this population remains uncertain.
